Neighborhood Launch Plan
One knock rarely wins a street. People need to see your name a few times before they trust it. This plan gives every home several friendly contacts over about two weeks: a visit, a note at the door, a letter, and a return visit. Pick a small area you can cover well, such as [STREET NAME] or one part of [NEIGHBORHOOD].

BEFORE YOU START

☐ Choose 40 to 80 homes and mark any that already have a new roof so you can skip them.
☐ Open your canvassing log in Archie. Every door gets a date, a time and a result.
☐ Pack door hangers, business cards and your phone for photos.

FIRST PASS

☐ Knock each door with The DOOR Opener.
☐ Nobody answers? Hang the Sorry We Missed You Door Hanger.
☐ That evening, mail the Sorry We Missed You Letter to each home you could not reach.

SECOND PASS, THREE OR FOUR DAYS LATER

☐ Go back to the homes you missed. Try a different time of day.
☐ Mention the note and the letter so they connect the dots.
☐ Still no answer? Leave a second hanger with a short handwritten line.

THIRD PASS, THE NEXT WEEK

☐ Try once more in person, or call if you have a number and consent to use it.
☐ Send the messages in Follow-Up Messages to every lead who talked with you but did not book.
☐ Move homes that said no thanks to a do-not-visit list and respect it.

NOTE: When a lead reaches the office by phone or web form, send the New Lead Confirmation Email the same hour.

REMINDER: Follow local soliciting rules, posted signs, and do-not-call and texting consent rules.

New Customer Checklist
Work through this list the same day the agreement is signed. A good first day keeps the job solid and opens the street around it.

WITH THE CUSTOMER

☐ Walk them through the next steps: who calls them, about when, and what they need to do.
☐ Send the New Customer Welcome Email before you drive away.
☐ Hand them the Referral Program Quick Card and tuck a second copy in their folder.
☐ Ask who they know that may need a roof looked at.
☐ Ask if a yard sign is fine with them. Place it only with a yes.
☐ Let them know other roofers may still knock, and that they can simply say they have chosen a company.

IF AN INSURANCE CLAIM IS INVOLVED

☐ Ask, with the customer's permission, for their agent's contact details and note them in Archie: [INSURANCE AGENT NAME], agency, number and email address.
☐ Email the agent a short hello, then follow with a call.

AROUND THE HOME

☐ Visit the Neighbor Ring using The DOOR Opener. Your reason for stopping is the job next door.
☐ Leave the Sorry We Missed You Door Hanger where nobody answers. A handwritten line about the nearby job helps, if the customer agrees to being mentioned.
☐ Mail the Sorry We Missed You Letter to those same homes.

Job Scheduled Checklist
Start this list as soon as the build has a date on the calendar. The days before a job are the easiest time to meet the people living nearby, because you have real news for them.

☐ Phone the customer with the planned date. Be honest that weather or material delivery can move it.
☐ Follow the call with a written confirmation by email, and add a friendly line about referrals.
☐ Ask whether they know the people next door by name, and whether you may say you are working for them.
☐ Bring up the Referral Program Quick Card they already have.
☐ Go over what to move or protect: cars, patio items, pets, wall hangings.

IF AN INSURANCE AGENT IS IN THE LOOP

☐ Send the agent a short update with the build date, only if they answered your first message.

TELL THE NEIGHBORS

☐ Mail the Neighbor Ring Notice to homes close enough to hear the work.
☐ Visit those homes during the week before the build. Open with The DOOR Opener and the news about the job.
☐ Nobody home? Leave a copy of the notice at the door.

Install Day Checklist
Use this list while the crew is on the roof. A working job site is your best proof, so be present and be seen.

WITH THE CUSTOMER

☐ Ask if they can point you to a neighbor or two by name.
☐ Mention the Referral Program Quick Card again.

ON THE STREET

☐ Walk the Neighbor Ring when most people are home. Use The DOOR Opener and point to the job in progress.
☐ Where nobody answers, leave the Neighbor Ring Notice. A handwritten note with the job address and your signature makes it personal.
☐ Log every door in Archie before you leave.

Insurance Agent Outreach Checklist
Use this list to meet local agents you have no tie to yet. The goal is a helpful working relationship, built slowly.

BUILD YOUR LIST

☐ Send one follow-up email a week later with something helpful, like a seasonal roof care tip sheet.
☐ Call one more time, then move them to a quarterly check-in.

IMPORTANT: You document roofs and explain what you find. Coverage is always decided by the insurance company. Never ask an agent to steer a claim.

Sales System Overview
This page shows how every part of the Archie Sales Playbook fits together. Read it once from top to bottom. After that, come back when you are not sure what to do next with a street or a customer.

THE BIG IDEA

Roofing sales has two engines. The first engine opens a neighborhood where nobody knows you yet. The second engine turns each signed customer into more conversations nearby. Most reps only run the first one. The reps who earn the most run both, every week.

Neither engine depends on clever lines. Both depend on showing up several times, being useful, and writing down what happened.

ENGINE ONE: OPENING A NEIGHBORHOOD

Use the Neighborhood Launch Plan. In short:

1. Pick a small group of homes you can cover fully.
2. Knock with The DOOR Opener.
3. When somebody answers and is interested, look at the roof and run The ROOFTOP Visit.
4. When nobody answers, leave the Sorry We Missed You Door Hanger and mail the Sorry We Missed You Letter that night.
5. Return a few days later at a different hour and mention the note you left.
6. Try a third time, in person or by phone where the rules allow.
7. Keep in touch with every open lead using Follow-Up Messages.

TIP: Mornings, early evenings and Saturdays reach different people. Changing the hour matters more than changing the words.

ENGINE TWO: THE CUSTOMER JOURNEY

Each customer passes through five moments. Every moment gives you an honest reason to talk with the customer and with the homes around them. Each one has its own checklist in this playbook.

Moment 1, Signed

• Explain next steps and send the New Customer Welcome Email.
• Hand over the Referral Program Quick Card.
• With permission, greet their insurance agent if a claim is part of the job.
• Visit the Neighbor Ring for the first time.

Moment 2, Scheduled

• Call and email the customer with the build date.
• Mail the Neighbor Ring Notice so nearby homes know work is coming.
• Knock those doors during the week before the build.

Moment 3, Install Day

• Be on site. Check in with the customer and crew.
• Ask the customer for an introduction to someone next door.
• Walk the Neighbor Ring while the job is visible.

Moment 4, Install Complete

• Do the final walk and send a completion note.
• Mail a finished-job letter to the same nearby homes.
• Knock again. People like to see the result.

Moment 5, Paid in Full

• Send a thank you card.
• Ask for a review with Review Request Messages.
• Schedule three check-ins over the next three months.
• Make one last pass through the Neighbor Ring.

Count it up. One customer gives you five reasons to speak with them and four or five reasons to visit each home close by. That is where steady referral business comes from.

WHERE THE TWO ENGINES MEET

Any conversation, from either engine, leads to the same place: a roof inspection followed by The ROOFTOP Visit. The Archie Sales Path walks through that appointment from the driveway to the signed agreement. Getting Invited In covers how to earn a seat inside. The Objection Handbook covers what to say when a homeowner hesitates.

WHAT TO TRACK

Good records are what make a second and third contact possible. Archie keeps them for you if you log as you go.

Door log

• Address, date and hour of each knock.
• Result: no answer, talked, booked, not interested, do not visit.
• Which hanger or letter was left.

Mail log for a new neighborhood

• Address and name if you have one. "Neighbor" works when you do not.
• Date and title of each letter, up to three.
• A skip list for homes with a new roof.

Mail log for each customer's Neighbor Ring

• The customer, their address and the build date.
• Each nearby address, with the date each of the three notices went out: signed, scheduled, complete.
• A skip list for current customers and homes that asked not to be contacted.

YOUR WEEK AT A GLANCE

• Daily: fill in the Daily Schedule Sheet and score yourself on the Daily Scorecard. Ten points is a good day.
• Daily: clear every checklist task due for your active customers before you knock new doors.
• Twice a week: return visits for homes on pass two or three of the Neighborhood Launch Plan.
• Weekly: check your numbers against your Earnings Plan and adjust how many doors you need.
• Monthly: reach out to partners with the Insurance Agent Outreach Checklist and the Real Estate Agent and Listed Homes Checklist.

HOUSE RULES

These protect you, your company and the homeowner.

• Be honest about why you are at the door. Never hint that you represent an insurer or any agency.
• Promise only what your company has put in writing.
• On insurance jobs, you document damage and explain what you found. You may meet the adjuster to point out what you documented. The insurance company decides coverage.
• Mention a customer by name or address only if they said you could.
• Honor no-soliciting signs and anyone who asks you not to come back.
• Calls and texts must follow do-not-call and consent rules. When unsure, ask your manager.

IF YOU ONLY REMEMBER THREE THINGS

1. Go back. The second and third visit do most of the work.
2. Every customer is a doorway to the homes around them, at all five moments.
3. Log it. If it is not in Archie, the follow-up will not happen.

DOCUMENTS IN THIS SYSTEM

• Sorry We Missed You Door Hanger
• Sorry We Missed You Letter
• Follow-Up Messages
• New Lead Confirmation Email

The appointment

• The Archie Sales Path
• Getting Invited In
• The ROOFTOP Visit and the ROOFTOP Quick Card
• Objection Handbook

After the sale

• New Customer Checklist and New Customer Welcome Email
• Job Scheduled Checklist and Neighbor Ring Notice

• Install Complete Checklist
• Review Request Messages, used with the Paid in Full Checklist
• Referral Program Quick Card

Running your business

docs.body:
The Archie Sales Path
This guide covers one appointment from start to finish: you arrive, you inspect, you explain, and the homeowner decides. It is the long version of The ROOFTOP Visit. Read this to understand why each part matters, then carry the ROOFTOP Quick Card in the field.

The path has seven stages. Do not skip ahead. Each stage earns the right to the next.

STAGE 1: ARRIVE AND ASK

Before a ladder comes off the truck, spend five minutes with the homeowner. Find out what they have noticed, how old the roof is, whether there have been leaks, and what made them agree to this visit. Ask how long they plan to stay in the house.

Listen for the main reason. It could be a stain on a bedroom ceiling, a sale coming up, or plain worry after a storm. Write it down. Everything later ties back to it.

Tell them what you are about to do and how long it should take, so nobody is left wondering.

STAGE 2: INSPECT FROM THE GROUND UP

Start on the ground. Circle the house the same direction each time so nothing gets missed. Look at:

• Siding, window trim, screens and soft metals for marks.
• Gutters and the ground under downspouts for loose granules.
• The lawn and beds for shingle pieces.
• Fascia, soffit and paint for water stains.

Then go up, if it is safe. From the eave, check how many layers are on the house and what is under the shingles at the edge. On the roof, work one slope at a time:

• Shingle surface: cracks, bruises, lifted tabs, missing pieces.
• Flashing at walls, chimneys and valleys.
• Pipe boots, vents and anything else that passes through the deck.
• Ridge and hip caps.
• Intake and exhaust ventilation.

Photograph wide, then close. A wide shot shows where. A close shot shows what. Record a short video summing up each slope in your own words. If the attic is easy to reach and the homeowner agrees, a quick look there can confirm leaks and airflow.

IMPORTANT: Report only what is really there. If the roof is in good shape, say so. An honest "you are fine for now" earns more referrals than a forced sale.

STAGE 3: SIT DOWN WITH THE PHOTOS

Come down and ask for a place to go through the pictures together.

"I took a lot of photos up there. They are easier to follow sitting down. Is there a table we could use for about twenty minutes?"

Hand them the phone or tablet. Start with the house from the street so they get their bearings. Then show the three or four findings that matter most, and lead with whatever connects to the main reason. For every photo, cover three points: what this is, why it matters, and what happens if it is left alone.

Skip the roofing slang. If you must use a trade word, explain it.

STAGE 4: LAY OUT THE CHOICES

Now explain what they can do. Usually there are a few paths: keep an eye on it, repair, replace, or, when a storm is involved, contact their insurance company and let it decide.

Say plainly that the decision is theirs:

"Let me show you the options as I see them, including the ones that do not involve hiring us. My job right now is to make sure you understand your roof."

If insurance is part of it, describe your role accurately. You document, you explain, and you can be there when the adjuster inspects to point out what you recorded. Whether anything is covered is the insurer's call.

Then stop and invite questions. Answer each one fully before moving on. A question now is far better than a doubt later.

STAGE 5: SHOW WHY YOUR COMPANY FITS

Only after the roof is understood do you talk about your company. Open the Presentation Binder and keep it short.

• Begin with nearby work and reviews from customers who agreed to be shared.
• Explain how a job runs, from material delivery to cleanup.
• Share the facts your company has in writing: [INSERT CREDENTIALS] and a workmanship warranty of [INSERT WARRANTY LENGTH].
• Pick one strength that speaks to the main reason and spend the most time there.

Present your recommendation and the price. Go line by line so the number is never a mystery.

STAGE 6: ASK, THEN LISTEN

Check where they stand with an open question:

"Now that you have seen the roof and the plan, what matters most to you in picking who does the work?"

[LET THEM ANSWER FULLY]

If your company truly meets what they describe, say how, with specifics. Then ask directly:

"It sounds like we are a good match for that. Would you like us to take care of this for you?"

[STAY QUIET AND WAIT]

A yes moves you to Stage 7. Anything else is an objection or a need for time. Use Hear it, Check it, Answer it, Ask again from the Objection Handbook. If they still want time, respect it. Agree on a specific day to talk again and put it in Archie before you stand up.

NOTE: No pressure and no made-up deadlines. People who feel pushed tend to cancel.

STAGE 7: PAPERWORK AND NEXT STEPS

Go over the agreement in plain words before asking for a signature. Cover the scope, the price, the payment schedule and any cancellation rights. Let them read. Answer what they ask.

Then finish strong:

1. Confirm their best email and phone number, and how they like to be reached.
2. If a claim is involved and they are willing, note their insurance agent's contact details.
3. Spell out what happens next, who will be in touch, and roughly when.
4. Book your next check-in so they are never left guessing.

Complete the New Customer Checklist the same day.

BEFORE YOU DRIVE AWAY

Two habits turn one sale into several.

Ask for an introduction

If the visit went well, ask:

"I have enjoyed this. Do you know the folks on either side of you? Would you be comfortable if I mentioned I am working with you?"

[WAIT FOR REPLY]

Some customers will offer to walk you over. Others will share a first name. Either helps. If they would rather not, thank them and leave it there.

Visit the Neighbor Ring

While you are still on the street, knock the homes beside, behind and across from your new customer using The DOOR Opener. You have a real, local reason to be there. Leave the Sorry We Missed You Door Hanger where no one answers and log each door in Archie.

docs.body:
Getting Invited In
Most roofing sales are decided at a table, not on a porch. At a table the homeowner can see photos, ask questions and think. On a porch they are half listening and ready to shut the door. This guide explains why reps get stuck outside and three honest habits that earn a seat inside.

WHY REPS GET STUCK AT THE DOOR

The usual cause is a memorized speech. It sounds the same at every house: a name, a company, a line about storms, an offer to look at the roof, and a hopeful "does that work?"

That speech fails for a simple reason. It assumes every homeowner is in the same spot, and they are not. Think about who might open the door:

• Someone who has no idea whether the roof has a problem.
• Someone who already filed a claim and is waiting.
• Someone whose insurer paid for part of the roof.
• Someone whose claim was turned down.
• Someone who has money set aside and is comparing roofers.
• Someone with an old roof and no storm at all, who would be paying out of pocket.

An inspection offer only speaks to the first person. The others hear nothing meant for them, so they say no thanks.

People act when something matters to them. Your first job is to find out what that is.

HABIT 1: END YOUR OPENING WITH A QUESTION

Keep the greeting short, give your local reason for stopping, then ask something open. This is the third letter of The DOOR Opener. Good questions include:

"Have you had a chance to look at your roof since the storm on [STORM DATE]?"

"What have you noticed up there lately?"

"Has anyone been out to look at it yet?"

Then stop talking. A question hands the conversation to the homeowner. Their answer usually tells you more in ten seconds than a speech would in two minutes.

HABIT 2: FIND OUT WHERE THEY STAND

Listen to the answer and place them in one of the situations above. Then respond to that situation and no other.

• Not sure about damage: offer [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A ROOF INSPECTION] and promise to show them photos either way.
• Claim filed, waiting: offer to document the roof so they have their own photos, and to be present when the adjuster visits if they would like.
• Paid in part or turned down: offer to look and explain what you see. Be clear that the insurance company decides coverage, and that you cannot change their decision.
• Funds in hand, shopping: skip the inspection talk. Ask what they are comparing and offer a written scope.
• Aging roof, no storm: talk about remaining life, repair against replacement, and payment choices your company offers.

When your offer matches their situation, they lean in. That is the moment an invitation becomes likely.

IMPORTANT: Never tell a homeowner what their policy covers or that a claim will be paid. You are a roofer, not an adjuster.

HABIT 3: BRING BACK SOMETHING WORTH SITTING DOWN FOR

Photos and video are your ticket inside. While you inspect:

• Take wide and close shots of every finding.
• Record a clip of under a minute explaining what you see.
• Note at least one helpful extra, such as a clogged gutter, a loose cable, or a ball stuck behind the chimney. It shows you looked at the whole roof and not only at what sells.

When you come down, ask plainly:

"I have some photos and a short video to walk you through. It is a lot easier on a bigger screen at a table. Is there somewhere we could sit for a few minutes?"

[WAIT FOR REPLY]

Most people say yes, because now there is something real to look at. If they would rather stay outside, that is fine. Find shade, hold the screen where they can see, and go through the same photos. Never push to come in.

ONCE YOU ARE SEATED

• Thank them for the time.
• Put the device in their hands.
• Open with the main reason, the finding that matters most to them.
• Continue with The ROOFTOP Visit from the Findings step.

QUICK REVIEW

1. Ask, do not recite.
2. Match your offer to where they stand.
3. Earn the seat with photos, and ask for it honestly.

Practice these with a teammate until they feel natural. Role play each of the six homeowners above, taking turns at the door.

docs.body:
The ROOFTOP Visit

The ROOFTOP Visit is the order we follow at every roof appointment, storm or retail. Seven letters, seven parts. Do them in order and do not skip ahead to the price.

R IS FOR RAPPORT
• Arrive on time, smile, and use their name.
• Talk about them before you talk about roofs. The yard, the dog, how long they have lived here.
• Tell them what today will look like and about how long it takes.

O IS FOR OPEN QUESTIONS
Diagnose first. Ask, then listen, then write it down.
• "What made you want someone to look at the roof?"
• "Have you seen any leaks, ceiling stains or shingle grit in the gutters?"
• "How old is the roof, as far as you know?"
• Storm visit: "Have you talked to your insurance company yet, and what did they tell you?"
• Retail visit: "Are you getting other estimates?" and "Would paying monthly be helpful to hear about?"

O IS FOR ON THE ROOF
• Inspect only after the questions. Their answers tell you where to look.
• Take clear photos and short videos of everything, good and bad.
• Find the main reason. That is the single finding that matters most to this homeowner.

F IS FOR FINDINGS
• Sit down together somewhere shady or indoors so the screen is easy to see.
• Show the photos one at a time and say in plain words what each one means.
• Save the main reason for last and explain what happens if it is left alone.
• Storm visit: explain what storm damage looks like. Coverage is decided by the insurance company, not by you.
• Retail visit: explain what a complete roof job includes, so they can compare estimates fairly.

T IS FOR THE PLAN
• Your solution for this roof, tied to what they told you.
• Your process, step by step, from today to the final clean-up.
• Product choices and colors.
• Who you are: reviews, nearby jobs, [INSERT CREDENTIALS], warranty of [INSERT WARRANTY LENGTH].

O IS FOR OBJECTIONS AND THE ASK
• Ask, "What questions do you have for me?" Keep asking until there are none.
• For each worry, use Hear it, Check it, Answer it, Ask again. See the Objection Handbook.
• Then ask plainly: "Would you like us to take care of this for you?"
• If the answer is not yet, find out why, and book the follow-up day and time before you go.

P IS FOR PROMISE AND PASS-ALONG
• Promise the next step: what happens, who will call, and when.
• Tell them you hope to earn a great review when the job is done.
• Ask who else nearby might want a roof check. Share the Referral Program Quick Card.
• Storm visit: ask who their insurance agent is, so you know who to keep informed.

REMINDER: Never tell a homeowner what their policy pays for, and never promise a claim result.

docs.body:
ROOFTOP Quick Card

Print this and keep it on your clipboard. It is the short version of The ROOFTOP Visit. One glance before you ring the bell, one glance before you leave.

THE SEVEN PARTS IN ONE LINE EACH
1. Rapport. Be a guest first and a roofer second.
2. Open questions. Why did they call, what have they noticed, what worries them.
3. On the roof. Photos and video of everything. Spot the main reason.
4. Findings. Show the pictures in the shade. Plain words. Main reason last.
5. The plan. Your fix, your steps, product choices, proof you do good work.
6. Objections and the ask. Answer every worry, then ask for the job.
7. Promise and pass-along. Name the next step. Ask who else you can help.

THREE QUESTIONS YOU MUST ASK
• "What have you noticed that made you want this looked at?"
• "Is anyone else part of this decision?"
• "What matters most to you in choosing a roofer?"

STORM OR RETAIL
• Storm: ask where they stand with their insurance company. You document and explain. The insurance company decides coverage.
• Retail: ask about other estimates and whether monthly payments would help.

WHEN A WORRY COMES UP
Hear it. Check it. Answer it. Ask again.

THE ASK
"Does this plan make sense to you? Then let's get your name on the paperwork and get you on the schedule."

BEFORE YOU DRIVE AWAY
• Next step set, with a day and time
• Photos saved to the job
• Notes typed in while they are fresh
• Asked for one neighbor or friend to talk to
• Thanked them, whatever the answer was

TIP: If you only remember one thing from this card, remember to ask questions before you climb the ladder. Diagnose first.

NOTE: Make no promise about claims, policies or deductibles. Only say what your company has approved.

The DOOR Opener

A four-part way to start a friendly talk at any front door. It fits storm work and normal retail days. Learn the four parts, then say them in your own words. Keep a copy in your truck.

THE FOUR PARTS

D: Drop the Pressure

• Smile, say hello, give your first name, then take a step back from the door.
• Sample: "Hi there, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. Sorry to pop up on you."

O: Our Reason for Being Here

• Give one true local tie: a job close by, a storm date, or the street itself.
• Sample: "We are doing some roof work for [NEIGHBOR'S NAME] a few doors down."

O: One Open Question

• Ask something that cannot be answered with yes or no. Then be quiet and listen.
• Sample: "What have you noticed up top since the storm on [STORM DATE]?"

R: Respond With a Simple Offer

• Match your offer to what they just told you. Keep it small and easy to say yes to.
• Sample: "That makes sense. Would it help if I did [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A ROOF INSPECTION] while our crew is on [STREET NAME]?"

TIP: If the answer is no, thank them and move on. A kind goodbye today can turn into a phone call next month.

docs.body:
Door Openers for Canvassing

These are short ways to start a talk at the front door. Each one follows The DOOR Opener: drop the pressure, give our reason for being here, ask one open question, then respond with a simple offer. You are not selling a roof on the porch. You are earning a short visit.

HOW TO USE THIS PAGE

• Pick the group that fits what is going on in the neighborhood today.
• Read the lines out loud until they sound like you. Swap any word that feels stiff.
• Only say things that are true. If you have not worked for a neighbor, use the street or the storm date as your reason.
• After your question, stop talking. Let the homeowner finish.
• Their answer tells you which offer to make. Do not make the offer first.

IMPORTANT: You are a roofer, not an insurance adjuster. You can document damage and explain what you found. The insurance company decides what is covered. Never promise that a claim will be approved or paid, and never tell a homeowner what their policy says.

RIGHT AFTER A STORM

Use these in the first days, when most people have not looked at their roof yet.

Opener 1: The Neighbor's Roof

"Hi, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. I'll be quick."
[STEP BACK FROM THE DOOR]
"We were just up on [NEIGHBOR'S NAME]'s roof checking what the storm on [STORM DATE] did. Since I'm on [STREET NAME] anyway, I wanted to say hello."
"What did that storm look like from your house?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Thanks for telling me. Would it help if I looked at your roof and showed you photos of what is up there?"

Opener 2: The Street

"Good afternoon. I'm [YOUR NAME], I work for [COMPANY NAME] here in [CITY, STATE]."
[SMILE AND STEP BACK]
"A lot of roofs in [NEIGHBORHOOD] took hail on [STORM DATE]. Some came through fine and some did not. From the ground it is hard to tell which is which."
"What have you been able to see on yours so far?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Got it. I can go up, take pictures, and show you exactly what I find. Then you decide what, if anything, to do."

Opener 3: The Honest Unknown

"Hi, sorry to bother you. I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]."
"I'm checking roofs on this block after the wind we had on [STORM DATE]. I don't know yet if yours has a problem, and I would not guess from the sidewalk."
"When did someone last get up there and look?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Then a quick look could give you peace of mind either way. I have time today or [DATE AND TIME]. Which is easier?"

WHEN A CLAIM IS ALREADY OPEN

Use these a few weeks in, when adjusters have been through the area and people are waiting or unsure.

Opener 4: Where Things Stand

"Hi, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. We are working with a few families on [STREET NAME] since the storm."
"I'm not here to push anything. I'm just checking in with the neighbors while we are close by."
"Where do things stand with your roof right now?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"That helps. If you like, I can document what is on the roof with photos, so you have your own record to look at next to the adjuster's report."

Opener 5: The Adjuster Visit

"Hello, I'm [YOUR NAME] from [COMPANY NAME]. Quick question, then I'll let you go."
"We have met several adjusters on roofs around [NEIGHBORHOOD] this month to point out what we photographed."
"What happened when your insurance company came out?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Thank you. I can't speak for your insurance company, they make the call on coverage. What I can do is look at the roof and explain in plain words what I see."

WHEN THE ANSWER FROM INSURANCE WAS NOT WHAT THEY HOPED

Use these with care. People may be upset. Listen first. Do not promise a different result.

Opener 6: A Second Set of Eyes

"Hi, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. Do you have one minute?"
"Some folks around here were told their roof had little or no storm damage, and they are not sure what to make of that."
"What were you told about yours?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"I understand. I can't change what the insurance company decides. I can inspect the roof, take clear photos, and tell you honestly what I find. If there is nothing there, I will say so."

Opener 7: Repair Without a Claim

"Good morning. I'm [YOUR NAME], I'm with [COMPANY NAME]."
"We are helping a few of your neighbors who chose to fix their roofs on their own, without going through insurance."
"What is your plan for the roof this year?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Makes sense. I can look it over and lay out your choices, from a small repair to a full roof, so you can compare."

WHEN THEY ARE READY TO PICK A ROOFER

Use these late in a storm season, when many homeowners already have an answer from insurance and need the work done.

Opener 8: The Yard Sign

"Hi, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. You may have seen our sign at [NEIGHBOR'S NAME]'s place."
"We are putting their new roof on [DATE], so there will be a truck and some noise that day. I wanted you to hear it from me first."
"How far along are you with your own roof?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Good to know. If you are still choosing a roofer, I would be glad to sit down, look at your paperwork with you, and show you how we would do the job."

Opener 9: Choosing a Contractor

"Hello, I'm [YOUR NAME] from [COMPANY NAME], a local roofer."
"Quite a few homes on this street are getting new roofs this season, and we are doing some of them."
"What matters most to you in the company that does yours?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"That is a fair thing to care about. Let me show you how we handle that. Would [DATE AND TIME] work for a short visit?"

NO STORM, JUST A NORMAL DAY

Use these for retail canvassing around a job you are already doing.

Opener 10: The Job Next Door

"Hi, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. We are the crew working at [NEIGHBOR'S NAME]'s house."
"I'm letting the neighbors know what we are doing and when we will be finished."
"How old is the roof on your home, if you know?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Thanks. While our ladders are out, I can offer [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A ROOF INSPECTION]. No pressure at all."

Opener 11: The Small Thing You Saw

"Hi there, I'm [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. I'm working up the street."
"Walking by, I saw [WHAT YOU SAW FROM THE GROUND] on your roof. It may be nothing, but I would want someone to tell me."
"What do you know about that spot?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"I can take a closer look and send you a photo so you can see it yourself."

SETTING THE VISIT

When they say yes, lock in the details before you leave the porch.

1. Offer two times and let them choose.
2. Ask who else helps make decisions about the house, and invite them.
3. Get the best phone number and ask if texting is okay.
4. Say what will happen: you inspect, you show photos, you explain, they decide.
5. Write it in Archie right away, then leave a card.

WHEN THEY SAY NO

"No problem at all. Thanks for your time. Here is my card in case anything changes."

NOTE: Skip any home with a no soliciting sign, and follow the canvassing rules of the city or neighborhood you are working in.

Homeowner Cold Call Script

Use this when you phone a homeowner who has not asked to hear from you. The goal of the call is small: start a real talk and, if it fits, book a roof visit. Do not try to sell a roof by phone.

BEFORE YOU DIAL

• Know why you are calling this home. A job close by, a storm date, or their street.
• Have two open times on your calendar ready to offer.
• Stand up and smile. People can hear it.

IMPORTANT: Your company must follow do-not-call rules and texting consent rules. Only call numbers your company has cleared, and stop right away if someone asks you not to call again. Ask your manager if you are unsure.

THE CALL IN FOUR PARTS

The phone version of The DOOR Opener: lower the pressure, say why you are calling, ask one open question, then make a simple offer.

Part 1: Lower the Pressure

"Hi, is this [HOMEOWNER NAME]?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"This is [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME], a roofer here in [CITY, STATE]. You were not expecting my call, so I will keep it to a minute. Is now okay?"
[IF NOT, ASK FOR A BETTER TIME AND CALL BACK THEN]

Part 2: Say Why You Are Calling

Pick the one that is true for this home.

Near a job:
"We are working on a roof for [NEIGHBOR'S NAME] on [STREET NAME], and I am calling a few of the homes around it."

After a storm:
"We have been checking roofs in [NEIGHBORHOOD] since the storm on [STORM DATE], and your street is on our list."

Normal day:
"We look after a number of roofs in [NEIGHBORHOOD], and many homes there are reaching the age where roofs need attention."

Part 3: Ask One Open Question

Choose one. Then listen without cutting in.

"What have you noticed about your roof lately?"
"How did your home come through that storm?"
"What is the story with your roof, as far as you know?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]

Part 4: Make a Simple Offer

Tie the offer to what they said.

If they are not sure about the roof:
"That is common. I could come by, get up there, and show you photos of what I find. Then you will know."

If an insurance claim is in progress:
"Thanks for sharing that. I can't speak for your insurance company, coverage is their decision. I can document the roof and explain what I see in plain words."

If they already plan to replace or repair:
"Good timing then. I would be glad to look it over and lay out your choices so you can compare."

BOOKING THE VISIT

"I have [DATE AND TIME] or [DATE AND TIME]. Which suits you better?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Great. Will anyone else who helps decide things about the house be home then?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Let me read the address back to be sure: [CUSTOMER ADDRESS]. Is that right?"
"Where should I send a confirmation, email or text?"
[GET THE EMAIL OR NUMBER. ASK BEFORE YOU TEXT]
"You are all set. I will see you on [DATE AND TIME]. Thank you, [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME]."

IF THEY SAY NO THANKS

"I understand. Thanks for taking my call. Would you like me to take you off our list?"
[DO WHAT THEY ASK AND NOTE IT IN ARCHIE]

IF YOU GET VOICEMAIL

"Hi [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME], this is [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME]. We are doing roof work near [STREET NAME] and I had a quick question about your roof. My number is [YOUR PHONE]. Again, [YOUR NAME] at [YOUR PHONE]. Thanks."

TIP: One short voicemail is enough. Do not leave a second one the same week.

EMAIL TO SEND AFTER A CALL

Use this when the homeowner asked you to send something in writing, or gave you their email on the call.

Subject: Your roof on [STREET NAME]

Hi [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME],

Thanks for talking with me today. As promised, here is a short note about who we are.

[COMPANY NAME] is a local roofing company serving [CITY, STATE]. We have been working with homeowners in [NEIGHBORHOOD], and here is what a visit from us looks like:

• We inspect the roof and take photos.
• We show you those photos and explain them in plain words.
• We lay out your choices and answer your questions.
• You decide what happens next. There is no pressure from us.

If your roof was hit by a storm and you are thinking about an insurance claim, we can document what we find. Your insurance company decides what is covered.

About us: [INSERT CREDENTIALS]

If you would like to set a time, just reply here or call me at [YOUR PHONE].

Thank you,
[YOUR NAME]
[TITLE]
[COMPANY NAME]
[YOUR PHONE]

docs.body:
Inbound Lead Scripts: Phone and Web

These people reached out to you first. That makes them your best leads. Your job on this call is to be warm, learn enough to send the right person, and book the visit. Save the roof talk for the home.

IN THIS DOCUMENT

• Script A: Someone calls the office
• Script B: You call back a web form or online lead
• The Roof Questions (used by both scripts)
• Booking the Visit (used by both scripts)
• After You Hang Up

SCRIPT A: SOMEONE CALLS THE OFFICE

"Thanks for calling [COMPANY NAME]. This is [YOUR NAME]. What can I do for you today?"
[LISTEN. LET THEM FINISH. WRITE DOWN THEIR OWN WORDS]
"I'm glad you called. We can help with that. Can I get your first and last name?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Thanks, [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME]. What is a good number for you if our call drops?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Is it okay if we text that number about your appointment?"
[NOTE YES OR NO IN ARCHIE]
"To send the right person out, I need to learn a little about the roof. It takes about two minutes."
[GO TO THE ROOF QUESTIONS]

SCRIPT B: YOU CALL BACK A WEB LEAD

TIP: Call as fast as you can. A lead called back within minutes is far more likely to pick up than one called the next day.

"Hi, may I speak with [HOMEOWNER NAME]?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"This is [YOUR NAME] at [COMPANY NAME]. I'm calling because you sent us a request through [WHERE THE LEAD CAME FROM] a little while ago about [WHAT THEY ASKED FOR]. Did I catch you at an okay time?"
[IF NOT, SET A CALLBACK TIME AND KEEP IT]
"Thank you for getting in touch. I want to make sure we send the right person, so I have a few quick things to ask about the roof."
[GO TO THE ROOF QUESTIONS]

If they do not answer, leave one short voicemail:

"Hi [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME], it's [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME], returning your request about your roof. You can reach me at [OFFICE PHONE]. I will also try you again later today."

THE ROOF QUESTIONS

Ask these in a relaxed way. It should feel like a chat, not a form.

1. "What is the address of the property?"
2. "Are you the owner?"
3. "Is it a house, a townhome or condo, or a commercial building?"
4. "One story or more?"
5. "Do you know what the roof is made of? Shingles, metal, tile, something else?"
6. "Tell me what is going on with it."
7. "How long has this been happening, and what have you done about it so far?"

Listen closely on the last one. Their answer tells you what kind of visit this is.

• Everyday roofing: They may be collecting estimates, planning ahead, or dealing with a leak that cannot wait. Mark urgent leaks as urgent.
• Storm related: They may not know if there is damage, may have a claim open, or may already have an answer from their insurance company. Write down where they are. Do not give opinions about coverage. That is the insurance company's decision.

Then ask:

8. "How did you hear about us?"
[THANK THEM AND REPEAT BACK WHAT THEY SAID]

Optional, for everyday roofing only:

9. "Some homeowners like to know about payment plans. Should I have your rep bring that information?"
[IF YES, NOTE IT. THE REP WILL EXPLAIN THE OPTIONS AT THE VISIT]

BOOKING THE VISIT

"Let's find a time. The visit goes best when everyone who helps decide about the home can be there, so all the questions get answered at once. Does that work for you?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Our first opening is [DATE AND TIME]. I also have [DATE AND TIME]. Which would you like?"
[IF NEITHER WORKS, ASK WHAT DAY SUITS THEM AND FIND THE CLOSEST OPENING]
"Perfect. Let me read the address back: [CUSTOMER ADDRESS]."
"What email should I send the confirmation to?"
[READ THE EMAIL BACK LETTER BY LETTER]

Now tell them what to expect:

"Here is how it will go. You will get a confirmation from us shortly. [YOUR NAME OR THE REP'S NAME] will come to your door and introduce themselves. They will look at the roof, show you photos of what they find, and walk through your choices. What you do after that is up to you. Any questions for me before we wrap up?"
[ANSWER OR NOTE QUESTIONS FOR THE REP]
"Thank you for choosing [COMPANY NAME], [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME]. We will see you [DATE AND TIME]."

AFTER YOU HANG UP

1. Enter the lead in Archie while it is fresh, with their own words about the problem.
2. Record whether they agreed to texts.
3. Send the New Lead Confirmation Email.
4. Flag anything urgent, such as water coming inside, to a manager right away.

REMINDER: Only text people who said yes to texting, and follow your company's do-not-call and texting consent rules.

Commercial Property Cold Call Script

Use this to reach the owner or manager of a commercial building, such as a shop, office, church, warehouse or apartment complex. The goal is one thing: a time to walk the roof with the person who makes decisions.

IMPORTANT: Follow your company's do-not-call rules. You are a roofer, not an insurance adjuster. Do not promise that insurance will pay for anything. The insurance company decides coverage.

STEP 1: FIND THE RIGHT PERSON

"Hello, this is [YOUR NAME] with [COMPANY NAME], a roofing company in [CITY, STATE]. Who looks after building maintenance for [PROPERTY ADDRESS]?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
[IF IT IS SOMEONE ELSE, ASK FOR THEIR NAME, NUMBER AND EMAIL]
[THANK THE PERSON WHO HELPED YOU]

STEP 2: GIVE YOUR REASON

"Thanks for taking a minute. I work on roofs in [NEIGHBORHOOD], and from the parking lot at your building I could see [WHAT YOU SAW FROM THE GROUND]. I thought you would want to know."

STEP 3: ASK ONE OPEN QUESTION

Choose the one that fits.

No recent storm:
"Who checks the roof for you now, and how often?"

A storm came through:
"How did the building hold up in the storm on [STORM DATE]?"

They mention an insurance claim:
"Where is that claim today?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY. TAKE NOTES]

STEP 4: MAKE THE OFFER

"Here is what I can do. I will walk the roof, take photos and video, and send you a short written summary of its condition. You can keep it for your records, or share it with your insurance company if you choose to. What they do with it is their call."

If they already plan to replace the roof:
"We work on [TYPE OF BUILDING] roofs often. I would be glad to look at yours and put a proposal together for you to compare."

STEP 5: SET THE TIME

"Would [DATE AND TIME] or [DATE AND TIME] be better for a roof walk?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Is there roof access I should know about, and should anyone else be there?"
"What email should I send the confirmation to?"
"Thank you. I will see you then."

NOTE: Commercial decisions often involve more than one person. Ask who else will want to see the report, and log every name in Archie.

Insurance Agent Introduction Call

Local insurance agents talk to homeowners every day. An agent who trusts you may send people your way for a long time. This call is how you start that friendship. Make it after you have sent a short hello by email.

WHERE TO FIND AGENTS

• Ask each customer, with their permission, who their agent is.
• Look up home and business insurance offices near the areas you work.
• Start with a short list. Five good relationships beat fifty names.

IMPORTANT: You are a roofer, not a public adjuster. Do not offer to manage or argue anyone's claim. Coverage is decided by the insurance company. Share customer details with an agent only when the customer has said yes.

THE CALL

"Hi [INSURANCE AGENT NAME], this is [YOUR NAME] from [COMPANY NAME]. I sent you an email on [DATE]. Do you have two minutes?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"I know roofers call your office all the time asking for leads. I would rather start by asking what would be useful to you."
"When one of your clients has a roof problem, what do you wish the roofer would do better?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY. WRITE DOWN WHAT THEY SAY]
"That is helpful, thank you. Here is how we try to work."

Then share the points that match what they told you:

• We take clear photos of every roof and give the homeowner a copy.
• We explain what we found in plain words and leave coverage questions to the insurance company.
• With the homeowner's okay, we keep their agent informed on when work starts and when it is done.
• When a client of yours calls us, we call back within [YOUR RESPONSE TIME].
• We remind customers to talk with their own agent about any policy questions.

"Would it be worth meeting for a few minutes so you can see a sample of our photo reports?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]

IF YES

"Great. Would [DATE AND TIME] or [DATE AND TIME] suit you? I can come to your office."
[CONFIRM THE TIME. BRING SAMPLE REPORTS AND BUSINESS CARDS]

IF NOT NOW

"No problem. May I check back in a couple of months? In the meantime, my number is [YOUR PHONE] if a client ever needs a roof looked at."

TIP: After you meet, send a thank-you note the same day. Small, steady contact builds trust.

Real Estate Agent Listing Call

Use this to phone the agent on a home that is for sale when you have a real reason to think the roof needs a look. Roof trouble found late can slow a sale. An early inspection lets the agent and seller deal with it on their own schedule.

NOTE: Only call about a roof you have truly seen from the street. Say what you saw, not what you guess. Follow your company's do-not-call rules.

Follow-Up Messages

Most homeowners do not decide on the first visit. A calm, helpful check-in keeps you in the picture. Use these after The ROOFTOP Visit when the homeowner needed time. Pick one way to reach out per day, not all three.

BEFORE YOU REACH OUT

• Look at your notes in Archie. What was the main reason they wanted the roof looked at?
• What were they waiting on? A talk with a spouse, another estimate, an answer from insurance?
• Have something useful to add, such as a photo, an answer to a question they asked, or an open date.

REMINDER: Text only people who agreed to get texts, and follow your company's do-not-call and texting consent rules. If someone asks you to stop, stop.

[WAIT FOR REPLY]

docs.body:
Objection Handbook

An objection is not a door slamming. It is a homeowner telling you what they still need before they can say yes. This handbook gives you one simple method and plain answers for the worries you will hear most.

WHY PEOPLE PUSH BACK
A roof is a big decision and most people make it once or twice in a lifetime. When they hesitate, one of these is usually behind it:
• They are not sure about you or your company yet.
• They are not sure the roof really has a problem.
• They are not sure about the cost or how to pay.
• They are not sure the timing is right, or someone else needs to weigh in.

Your first job is to work out which one it is. The words they use do not always match the real worry. "Let me think about it" could be any of the four.

THE METHOD
Hear it, Check it, Answer it, Ask again.

1. Hear it. Stop talking. Let them finish. Nod. Do not jump in with an answer you have ready.
2. Check it. Say it back in your own words and ask if you have it right. Then ask if there is anything else on their mind.
3. Answer it. Give a short, honest answer to the real worry. Use a photo, a review or a fact, not a speech.
4. Ask again. Once the worry is settled, go back to your question. Many reps answer well and then forget to ask.

TIP: Step 2 is where most sales are saved. When people feel understood, they relax, and the real worry comes out.

WORRIES ABOUT YOU

"I have never heard of your company."
[NOD AND SMILE]
"That is fair. You should know who is working on your home. Is it mostly that we are new to you, or is there something else too?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Here are our reviews, and here are a few homes we have done near [STREET NAME]. You are welcome to call any of them. Does that help?"

"I already have a roofer."
"Good, it sounds like you have someone you trust. Has he been up there since the last storm?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Would a second set of photos hurt? You can share them with him."

"I need to talk it over with my spouse."
"Of course. This is a decision for both of you. What do you think they will want to know?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"Let me leave the photos with you. Better yet, when are you both home? I can walk you both through it in about 15 minutes."

WORRIES ABOUT THE ROOF

"My roof looks fine from here."
"It may well be fine. Most problems cannot be seen from the ground, which is why I take pictures. If it is in good shape I will tell you so, and you will have photos for your records. Is it all right if I take a look?"

"It is not leaking."
"I am glad to hear that. A roof often has trouble for a long time before water shows up inside. Let me show you this photo of the main reason I am concerned. What do you see here?"

"We are selling the house soon."
"That is useful to know. A buyer's inspector will look at the roof closely. Would it help to know what they will find before they do?"

WORRIES ABOUT MONEY

"Your price is higher than the other estimate."
"Thank you for telling me. Can we look at the two side by side? I want to be sure we are comparing the same job."
[COMPARE LINE BY LINE: TEAR-OFF, FLASHING, VENTS, CLEAN-UP, WARRANTY]
"Here is what is in ours that I do not see in theirs. Knowing that, which job do you want on your home?"

"I cannot afford this right now."
"I understand. A roof is a lot of money. Is it the total, or the idea of paying it all at once?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY]
"We have payment options through [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A FINANCING PARTNER]. Would it help to see what that looks like per month?"

"Just leave me a number."
"I will. So the number is right, I need to measure and take a few photos first. Otherwise I am guessing, and a guess is no good to either of us. May I?"

"Another roofer said they would pay my deductible for me."
"I have heard that too. We do not do it, and in many places it is against the law. Your deductible is part of your agreement with your insurance company. What I can promise is honest paperwork and good work. Is the deductible the main thing holding you back?"

WORRIES ABOUT TIMING

"Let me think about it."
"Sure. This is not something to rush. So I can leave you with the right information, what part are you still weighing? The company, the roof itself, or the cost?"
[WAIT FOR REPLY, THEN ANSWER THAT ONE THING]

"We want to get more estimates."
"That is smart. Here is a short list of things to ask every roofer, so the estimates are easy to compare. When do you expect to have them? I will call you on [DATE AND TIME] to answer anything that comes up."

"Call me in the spring."
"I can do that. One thing I would want to know in your shoes: is this something that can safely wait? Let me show you the photo again, and you decide."

WORRIES ABOUT INSURANCE

"I will just let my insurance company deal with it."
"That is a fine way to go, and the decision on coverage is theirs. What I do is the roofing side. I document what I found, and if you want, I meet the adjuster at your home to point out what is in my photos. Would it be useful to have a roofer there on that day?"

"I do not want my rates to go up."
"I understand that worry. I cannot tell you what your insurance company will do, and I would not want to guess. Your agent is the right person to ask. Would you like to call them before you decide anything?"

"The adjuster already said there is no damage."
"Thanks for telling me. I can only speak to what I saw on the roof. Here are my photos. If you think something was missed, you can ask your insurance company about a second look. That choice is yours and the decision is theirs."

IMPORTANT: You are a roofer, not an adjuster. Never say what a policy pays for, never promise a claim will be approved or paid, and never offer to negotiate or settle a claim for a homeowner. You document, you explain, and you can meet the adjuster to point out what you documented.

AT THE DOOR

"I am not interested."
[SMILE AND STEP BACK]
"No problem at all. Before I go, has anyone looked at your roof since the storm on [STORM DATE]?"
If the answer is still no, thank them and move on. A polite goodbye leaves the door open for next time.

"I am busy right now."
"I can see that. When would be a better time, later today or Saturday morning?"

FIVE HABITS THAT MAKE THIS EASIER
• Answer worries before they come up. If price is always raised, explain what goes into a roof during your plan.
• Keep answers short. Thirty seconds, then a question.
• Stay calm and kind. You are not arguing. You are helping someone decide.
• Use proof. Photos, reviews and nearby addresses do more than words.
• Know when to stop. If a homeowner says no twice after a fair answer, respect it. Leave your card and set a follow-up if they are open to one.

WHEN THE ANSWER IS STILL NO
Not every visit ends in a sale. Thank them for their time. Ask if you may check back after the next big storm. Log the worry in Archie so the next conversation starts where this one ended. See Follow-Up Messages for what to send.

PRACTICE
Pick the three worries you hear most. Write your own answer to each in your own words, using the four steps. Say them out loud with a teammate until they sound like you. The Role Play Practice Guide shows how to run that session.

REMINDER: Only say what is true and what your company has approved. An honest "I do not know, let me find out" builds more trust than a clever answer.

docs.body:
Role Play Practice Guide

Nobody wants to practice on a real homeowner. Role play lets a rep make mistakes in the office, where a mistake costs nothing. Ten minutes a day beats a long session once a month.

WHAT YOU NEED
• Two or three people: a rep, a homeowner and, if you can, a watcher who takes notes
• A timer
• A phone to record on, so the rep can hear how they sound
• This guide, The DOOR Opener and The ROOFTOP Visit

GROUND RULES
• Play it straight. The homeowner acts like a real person, not a comedian and not a bully.
• Finish the scene. If the rep stumbles, they keep going, just as they would on a porch.
• Keep scenes short. Three to five minutes is plenty.
• Kind and honest feedback only. Everyone takes a turn in every seat.

LEVELS OF DIFFICULTY

Level 1, Warm-Up

The rep knows the setting and knows which worry is coming. The goal is smooth words and a calm voice.

Level 2, Surprise

The rep knows the setting. The homeowner picks the worry in secret. The goal is listening.

Level 3, Open Scene

Nothing is agreed ahead of time. The homeowner decides who they are and how the day is going. The goal is to stay friendly and find the real worry.

Move up a level only when the level below feels easy.

HOW ONE ROUND WORKS
1. Set the scene in one sentence. Start the timer.
2. Run the scene to the end.
3. The rep speaks first: one thing that went well and one thing to change.
4. The homeowner says how it felt on their side of the door.
5. The watcher adds one thing that went well and one thing to change.
6. Run the same scene again right away, using the feedback.
7. Swap seats.

TIP: The second run is where the learning happens. Do not skip it to save time.

DOOR SCENES
Choose a reason for the knock, then a homeowner.

Reason for the knock:
• You are new to the street and a storm came through on [STORM DATE].
• A neighbor just hired your company. You are working the Neighbor Ring.
• A crew is on a roof three doors down today.
• A job nearby is finished and you are checking the street for stray nails.

Homeowner:
• Friendly and curious
• In a hurry, with dinner on the stove
• Has a brother-in-law who does roofs
• Was burned by a contractor before
• Says "not interested" before you finish your first sentence

What to watch for: Did the rep step back and drop the pressure? Did they give a local reason for being there? Did they ask one open question and make a simple offer?

STORM VISIT SCENES
The homeowner picks where they stand with their insurance company:
• Has not called them and is not sure there is any damage
• Called, and was told only part of the roof is included
• Called, and was told no
• Has been approved and is choosing a roofer

What to watch for: Did the rep ask questions before giving opinions? Did they stay on the roofing side, documenting and explaining, and leave coverage to the insurance company? A rep who promises a claim result fails the round, even if the rest was perfect.

RETAIL VISIT SCENES
The homeowner picks a reason for calling:
• The roof is old and they know it
• Water came through the ceiling last week
• They are remodeling and want the house to look better
• They may sell in a year or two
• They are collecting three estimates and yours is the second

What to watch for: Did the rep find out what matters most to this person? Did the plan they presented match it?

OBJECTION DRILLS
1. As a team, list the worries you hear most on a whiteboard.
2. The rep stands up. The team calls out one worry at a time.
3. The rep answers each one with Hear it, Check it, Answer it, Ask again.
4. Go around the room until every rep has faced every worry.

Good starter worries: the price, the spouse, more estimates, the roof looks fine, call me later. The Objection Handbook has sample answers. Reps should put them in their own words.

PHONE DRILLS
Sit back to back so you cannot see each other.
• A new lead calling in
• A call to confirm tomorrow's appointment
• A follow-up call a week after an estimate
• A check-in call with a past customer to ask for referrals

REMINDER: Before calling or texting real people, the company must follow do-not-call and texting consent rules.

FEEDBACK THAT HELPS
• Be specific. "You asked a great question about the leak" teaches more than "nice job."
• One change at a time. A rep cannot fix five things in the next run.
• Talk about what was said and done, not about the person.
• End on something that went well.

A SIMPLE SCORE SHEET
Give one point for each. Five is a great round.
• Friendly, relaxed opening
• Asked at least two open questions
• Let the homeowner finish talking
• Answered the real worry in under a minute
• Asked for a clear next step

A WEEKLY RHYTHM
• Monday: door scenes
• Tuesday: objection drills
• Wednesday: storm or retail visit scenes
• Thursday: phone drills
• Friday: open scenes, and each rep picks their weakest spot

NOTE FOR MANAGERS: Take a turn as the rep. When the team sees you practice, stumble and try again, they will do the same.

Your One-Sentence Introduction

When someone asks "What do you do?" you have about ten seconds. This guide helps you build one clear sentence that says who you help and what they get out of it. Use it at the door, on the phone, at a ball game or anywhere you meet people.

WHY ONE SENTENCE
• People decide fast whether to keep listening.
• "I sell roofs" is about you. A good introduction is about them.
• A sentence you have practiced comes out calm, even when you are nervous.

It is not a full pitch. Its only job is to earn the next minute of conversation. At the door it fits inside The DOOR Opener.

THE THREE BUILDING BLOCKS

Block 1, Who You Serve

Be specific. "Homeowners" is fine. "Homeowners on the east side with roofs over 15 years old" is better. Think about:
• The neighborhoods you work in
• The kind of building: houses, rentals, churches, small shops
• What is going on for them: a recent storm, an aging roof, a house going up for sale

Block 2, What Is On Their Mind

Write down what these people worry about. Use their words, not roofing words.
• "I do not know if the hail hurt my roof."
• "I am afraid of being overcharged."
• "I do not have time to deal with this."
• "I do not know which roofer to trust."
• "I do not want a mess in my yard."

Block 3, What They Walk Away With

This is the result, not the product. Nobody dreams about shingles. They want:
• A clear answer about the condition of their roof
• Photos they can keep
• A dry house and a quiet mind
• A job done right, with a tidy yard at the end
• Someone who calls back when they say they will

PUT IT TOGETHER
"I work with [WHO YOU SERVE] who [WHAT IS ON THEIR MIND], and I [WHAT THEY WALK AWAY WITH]."

Samples to get you started. Change them until they sound like you.
• "I work with homeowners around [NEIGHBORHOOD] who are not sure what the last storm did to their roof, and I show them with photos."
• "I look after older roofs in [CITY, STATE], so people know how many years they have left before it becomes a surprise."
• "I help busy families get roof work done without having to chase anybody. I keep them posted at every step."
• "I work with people getting ready to sell. I check the roof before the buyer's inspector does."

MAKE YOUR OWN
1. Write five answers for each block. Fifteen lines in all.
2. Mix and match until you have three sentences you like.
3. Say each one out loud. Cross out any word you would not use with a friend.
4. Pick one for storm work and one for retail work.
5. Try them on ten real people this week. Keep the one that gets "Oh, tell me more."

WHAT TO LEAVE OUT
• Promises about price, speed or insurance results. You are a roofer, not an adjuster, and coverage is decided by the insurance company.
• Big claims like "the best in town." Let your reviews say that.
• Roofing jargon. If a ten-year-old would not understand a word, swap it.

WHAT COMES NEXT
A good introduction ends with a question, so the other person gets to talk.
• "How old is your roof, do you know?"
• "Has anyone been up there since the storm?"
• "Who looks after your roof now?"

TIP: Practice in the truck before your first door each day. Three times out loud is enough to warm up.

docs.body:
What They Need and What They Want

Every homeowner you meet has two things going on. One is a problem with the roof. The other is how they hope the fix will go. Good reps listen for both.

THE NEED
The need is the plain problem. It is a fact you can photograph.
• Shingles are missing.
• Water is getting in around the chimney.
• The roof is 25 years old and worn thin.

Any decent roofer can meet the need. That is why the need alone rarely wins the job.

THE WANT
The want is personal. It is how this homeowner would like the whole thing to feel.
• "I want it done before my daughter's wedding."
• "I want to understand what I am paying for."
• "I do not want to take time off work."
• "I want the house to look sharp from the street."

Think of a toothache. The need is a filling. The want is a dentist who is gentle, explains things and sees you this week. You pick the dentist for the want.

HOW TO FIND BOTH
• The need shows up on the roof. Find it in your inspection and show it in photos.
• The want shows up in conversation. Ask, "What matters most to you about how this gets done?" Then stay quiet and listen.

USE WHAT YOU LEARN
When you present the plan, tie it to their want in their own words. "You said you cannot take time off, so here is how we keep you posted by text."

On storm visits, wants change with where the homeowner stands with their insurance company. Someone who has not called yet wants answers. Someone already approved wants a roofer they can count on. Ask before you assume.

TIP: Write the want in your Archie notes. It is the first thing to read before a follow-up call.

How to Explain What a Storm Roofer Does

After a storm, many homeowners think they only need a roofer on the day shingles go on. So they wait. This guide helps you explain, honestly, why it helps to have a roofer involved from the start.

THE HOMEOWNER'S PICTURE
Most people have never dealt with storm damage. They have questions like these:
• Is my roof actually damaged?
• How would I even know?
• What do I say when I call my insurance company?
• Who do I trust?

A roofer who only shows up to install cannot help with any of that. A roofer who knows storm work can help with the roofing side of all of it.

WHAT YOU CAN OFFER BEFORE ANY ROOF IS BUILT
• A careful inspection, with photos and video
• A clear explanation of what you found, in plain words
• A written record of the damage the homeowner can keep
• Being at the home when the adjuster visits, to point out what you documented
• Answers about materials, building code items and how the work is done
• A plan and a schedule if the roof does need work

WHAT YOU DO NOT DO
You are a roofer, not a public adjuster. So you never:
• Tell a homeowner what their policy pays for
• Promise a claim will be approved or paid
• Negotiate or settle a claim for them
• Offer to pay or reduce a deductible

The insurance company decides coverage. Say so out loud. It makes you more believable, not less.

HOW TO SAY IT
"A lot of folks call a roofer at the very end. I would rather help at the beginning. I will show you what is up there with photos. If you decide to call your insurance company, I can be here to point out what I found. What they decide is up to them. Either way, you will know where your roof stands."

TIP: Always start with what the homeowner needs and wants. See What They Need and What They Want.

How to Explain the Contingency Agreement

A contingency agreement is a short paper some roofing companies use on storm jobs. In plain words it says: if the insurance company approves the roof work, the homeowner will have this company do it. If the work is not approved, the agreement ends.

Explain it slowly and simply. For example:

"This says three things. One, you are fine with me being at your home when the adjuster visits, to point out what I documented. Two, if your insurance company approves the work, we are the roofer who does it, for the scope they approve plus any upgrades you choose. Three, if they do not approve it, this paper ends."

Then hand it over and let them read every line. Answer questions honestly. Never rush a signature.

IMPORTANT: Say only what your company's own agreement says. Do not promise an approval, a price or anything about the deductible. Cancellation rights differ by state, so use the form your company's attorney approved.

docs.body:
Insurance Contingency Agreement Outline

IMPORTANT: This is an outline, not a contract. It lists what an insurance contingency agreement usually includes. Your company's own attorney must write or review the real document before anyone uses it. Laws on these agreements differ from state to state.

WHAT THIS PAPER IS FOR
On a storm job, the homeowner agrees that if their insurance company approves the roof work, your company will do it. If the work is not approved, the agreement ends.

PARTS MOST AGREEMENTS INCLUDE

1. Who and Where
• Homeowner name, phone and email
• Property address: [CUSTOMER ADDRESS]
• Company name, address and license details: [COMPANY NAME], [INSERT CREDENTIALS]
• Date signed: [DATE]

2. Claim Details
• Insurance company name
• Claim number, if there is one yet
• Date of the storm: [STORM DATE]

3. What the Homeowner Allows
• The company may inspect and photograph the property.
• The company may be present when the adjuster visits and may talk with the insurance company about the roofing work itself, such as measurements, materials and building code items.
• Ask your attorney how to word this. A roofer is not a public adjuster and does not negotiate or settle claims.

4. The Condition
• The agreement depends on the insurance company approving the work.
• What happens if the work is not approved, or is approved only in part.

5. Scope and Price
• How the scope of work is set, usually from the approved insurance paperwork.
• How the price is set.
• How homeowner-chosen upgrades are priced and approved in writing.
• A plain statement that the deductible is owed by the homeowner.

6. Product Choices
• Shingle maker, style and color
• Drip edge and trim colors
• Gutters, siding or other items, if included
• A place for homeowner initials beside each choice

7. Payment
• When each payment is due
• How added insurance payments for extra approved work are handled

8. Cancellation
• The homeowner's right to cancel, the number of days and how to do it
• Any state-required notice, word for word as your attorney provides it

9. Other Terms Your Attorney May Add
• Warranty: [INSERT WARRANTY LENGTH]
• Scheduling and weather delays
• What happens if hidden damage is found
• How disagreements are settled

10. Signatures
• Homeowner signature and date
• Company representative signature and date: [YOUR NAME], [TITLE]

BEFORE YOU HAND IT OVER
• Use only the version your attorney approved.
• Fill in every blank. Leave nothing empty.
• Give the homeowner time to read it, and leave a copy with them.

See How to Explain the Contingency Agreement for what to say.

docs.body:
Presentation Binder Outline

A Presentation Binder is a set of pages you walk a homeowner through during the plan part of The ROOFTOP Visit. It keeps you on track and lets them see proof instead of just hearing it. Build it once, then keep it fresh.

PAPER OR SCREEN
• Paper: a clean binder with page protectors. Easy to hand across the table.
• Screen: slides on a tablet. Easy to update and to add job photos.
Either works. Pick the one you will keep neat and current.

WHAT GOES IN IT, IN ORDER

1. A Welcome Note
One short page from you to the homeowner. A sample is at the end of this outline.

2. Meet the Company
• Who owns it, where the office is, how long it has been around
• A team photo
• [INSERT CREDENTIALS]

3. Proof From Customers
• Real reviews, shown the way they look online
• Thank-you notes and messages, with the customer's permission
• Before and after photos of your own jobs

4. Jobs Near You
• A map or list of roofs you have done in and around [NEIGHBORHOOD]
• Street names are enough. Use a customer's name only if they said yes.

5. Paperwork That Protects the Homeowner
• Copies of the license and insurance documents your state calls for
• Maker certifications your company really holds

6. How a Roof Goes Together
• A simple picture of the layers: decking, underlayment, flashing, shingles, vents
• Photos of good work and of common shortcuts, so they can see the difference

7. Our Process
• Each step from signed paperwork to final walk-through
• Who their contact person is at each step
• How you protect the yard and clean up
• On storm jobs: what you do, such as documenting damage and meeting the adjuster, and a clear line that coverage is decided by the insurance company

8. Product Choices
• Shingle lines and colors, with samples if you have them
• Upgrades worth knowing about

9. Warranty
• Maker warranty and workmanship warranty: [INSERT WARRANTY LENGTH]
• Whom to call if something goes wrong

10. Ways to Pay
• Payment schedule
• Payment plan options, if your company has them: [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A FINANCING PARTNER]

11. Next Steps
• A blank copy of your agreement, so nothing is a surprise
• The Referral Program Quick Card

HOW TO USE IT

I could be wrong. I was looking from the ground. But it matched what wind usually does to a roof, so here is some background.

How Wind Hurts A Roof

Shingles are held down by nails and a strip of sealant. A hard gust can break that seal and lift a shingle. Sometimes the shingle tears off. More often it flaps, creases and settles back down. From the yard it looks normal. Up close, it is cracked along the fold.

Why It Matters

A creased or loose shingle no longer sheds water the way it should. Rain can get under it and reach the wood below. That kind of leak is slow. By the time a stain shows on a ceiling, the water has been coming in for a while.

• Shingles or pieces of shingle in the yard
• Tabs that look bent up or out of line
• Dark patches where a shingle is gone
• Metal trim along the edges that has pulled loose

I can get on the roof and look closely. I take photos and video of each area, then sit down and show them to you. If I was wrong and the roof is sound, you will hear that from me.

If wind did cause damage, you may want to talk with your insurance company. They decide what is covered. I can give you a clear record of what I found, and I can explain it to their adjuster if you ask me to.

• A different shingle that is close in size and color but not the same
• Leftover stock, if any can be found

60 Day Insurance Questions and Referral Email

NOTE: Send about 60 days after the job is paid in full.

Subject: Five questions to ask your insurance agent this year

Hi [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME],

Your roof is done, but I still think about the homes we have worked on. Something I see often is a homeowner who learns how their policy works only after a storm. That is a stressful time to find out.

I am a roofer, not an insurance agent, so I cannot tell you what your policy says. What I can do is hand you good questions. A ten minute call to your agent now can spare you a surprise later.

QUESTIONS FOR YOUR AGENT

1. How is my roof valued if it is damaged?
Some policies pay what a new roof costs. Others pay what the old roof was worth at its age, which is less. Ask which kind you have and how it changes as the roof gets older.

2. Does the way my roof is valued change at a certain age?
Many homeowners do not know that terms can shift once a roof passes a certain number of years. Ask if yours does, and when.

3. What happens if only part of the roof is damaged and the shingle color can no longer be bought?
Colors get discontinued. Ask how your policy treats a repair that would not match the rest of the roof, and if there is an add-on for that.

4. Are wind and hail treated differently from other damage?
In some areas these have their own deductible or their own limits. Ask so you know the number ahead of time.

5. Does my file show the new roof?
Send your agent the invoice and photos from our project. Ask if a new roof changes anything about your policy.

TIP: Write down the answers with the date and the name of the person you spoke with. Keep the note with your roof records.

If your agent asks for product names, install dates or photos, call me at [YOUR PHONE]. I am happy to send what we have on file for your home.

WHO ELSE COULD USE A STRAIGHT ANSWER?

docs.body:
90 Day Roof Care and Referral Email

NOTE: Send about 90 days after the job is paid in full.

Subject: A simple roof care routine for [CUSTOMER ADDRESS]

Hi [CUSTOMER FIRST NAME],

Three months have gone by since we finished your project. A new roof does not ask for much, but a little attention each season helps it last. Here is the routine I give to my own family.

AFTER EVERY BIG STORM

Walk around the house and look up from the ground. You are looking for shingles that are lifted, bent or missing, metal that has come loose, and dents in the gutters or downspouts. Check the yard for shingle pieces too. Please stay off the roof. It is easy to fall and easy to scuff the surface.

EVERY SPRING AND FALL

• Empty the gutters and downspouts. When they clog, water backs up under the roof edge and spills next to the foundation. If ladders are not your thing, hire someone.
• Brush off piles of leaves and pine needles, mostly in valleys and behind chimneys. Wet piles hold moisture against the shingles.
• Cut back branches that hang over or rub the roof. They scrape the surface and give squirrels a bridge.
• Peek in the attic with a flashlight on a sunny day and again after rain. Dark stains, damp insulation or daylight coming through all deserve a call.

WHAT TO AVOID

• Power washing. It strips the protective granules off shingles.
• Harsh cleaners. If you see dark streaks or moss, ask us what is safe for your roof type.
• Letting other trades walk on the roof without care. Satellite, solar and holiday light installers can cause damage. Ask them how they protect the roof.

TIP: Set two reminders on your phone, one for spring and one for fall. Small problems found early are usually small repairs.

If anything looks off, send me a photo at [YOUR PHONE]. I would rather look at ten false alarms than miss one real problem.

PASS IT ALONG

If these tips were useful, feel free to forward this email. And if someone you know is worried about their roof, I would be happy to help them the way we helped you. Reply with their name and number, once they say it is okay, and you receive [REFERRAL GIFT] as our thank you. You can refer as many people as you like.

Enjoy the season,

[EMAIL SIGNATURE]
