Still Deciding Email 2: Comparing Roofers on a Claim

NOTE: For a homeowner with a storm claim who met with you and has not chosen a roofer yet. Send it after the calls and texts in Follow-Up Messages, and after Still Deciding Email 1.

Subject: How to compare roofers when insurance is involved

Hi [HOMEOWNER NAME],

Choosing a roofer on an insurance job can feel confusing. It works differently from most purchases, and nobody hands you a rule book. Here are the things homeowners most often tell me they wish they had known sooner. I hope they help, no matter who you hire.

A FEW THINGS THAT SURPRISE PEOPLE

You choose the roofer.
In most cases the choice of contractor belongs to the homeowner. If you are not sure how it works for your policy, ask your insurance company or your agent.

The insurance company writes its own scope of work.
After the adjuster visits, the insurer usually prepares a written list of what it found and what it will pay toward. That list is where the conversation starts. Ask your adjuster how your claim will be paid out and when.

Not every bid is for the same job.
Two roofers can look at one house and write two very different plans. One may replace the flashing, vents and drip edge. Another may plan to reuse them. A lower number sometimes means less work, so line the bids up item by item.

The paperwork has to be true.
The invoice sent to an insurance company must match the work that was really done and the amount that was really charged. Walk away from anyone who offers to change those numbers or to make part of your cost disappear. That can put you at risk, not just the roofer.

QUESTIONS TO ASK ANY ROOFER

1. Will you give me a written scope that lists every item you will replace and every item you will reuse?
2. What products will you install, and what do the manufacturer's instructions and local building code require on my roof?
3. Who will be on site running the job, and how do I reach them?
4. What happens if you find rotted wood or hidden damage after tear-off?
5. Will you take photos of the work as it is done and share them with me?
6. What does your workmanship warranty include, and can I have it in writing?
7. Can I talk to two or three recent customers near me?

A roofer who is worth hiring will answer all seven without getting uneasy.

WHAT I CAN AND CANNOT DO

I can document the damage, explain what I found, and meet your adjuster at the house to point out what I documented. I cannot tell you what your policy says or what your insurance company will decide. Those answers come from them.

If you would like me to go through my scope with you one more time, or look over another bid next to mine, I am glad to do it. Reply here or call or text [YOUR PHONE].

Thank you,

[EMAIL SIGNATURE]

Insurance Agent Introduction Emails

WHO THIS IS FOR

Local property insurance agents you have not met yet. One agent who trusts you can send homeowners your way for a long time, so this is worth doing well and doing slowly.

HOW TO USE IT

• Build a short list of agents in your service area. Agency websites and business directories are good places to look.
• Ask each of your own customers who their agent is. A name you share is the best opener there is.
• Send Email 1. Wait about a week. If you hear nothing, send Email 2 once and then leave it alone.
• A phone call or a short visit to the office does more than any email. Use these to open the door, then show up in person.

IMPORTANT: Only an agent or the insurance company can explain a policy or decide coverage. Never tell an agent you will handle, negotiate or settle a claim. Your job is to inspect, document and do good work.

Hi [AGENT NAME],

My name is [YOUR NAME] and I work for [COMPANY NAME] here in [CITY, STATE]. You do not know me yet, so I will keep this short.

• We look at the roof and take dated photos of what we see.
• We explain what we found in plain words, including when we find nothing wrong.

• If they hire us, we keep them posted from the first visit to the final cleanup.

Thank you,
[EMAIL SIGNATURE]

Thank you,

Send this to the owner of a rental house or small rental building in a storm area. Owners often live somewhere else and do not see the roof for months, so a short, honest heads-up is welcome. County property records usually show the owner's mailing address. Call a few days after sending if you have a number.

IMPORTANT: Do not go on the roof or into the yard of a rental without the owner's permission. If the tenant is home, be polite, leave a card and ask who to contact.

Subject: Your rental on [STREET NAME] and the recent storm

Hi [LANDLORD NAME],

My name is [YOUR NAME], and I am a roofer with [COMPANY NAME]. I am writing about the house you own on [STREET NAME].

We have been working on that street since the [STORM TYPE] on [STORM DATE]. Several of your neighbors there have had their roofs looked at. Since you may not be at the property often, I thought you would want to know.

To be clear, I have only seen your roof from the sidewalk. I am not telling you it is damaged. I am saying it is worth a look.

Why it matters more on a rental:

• You are not there when it rains, so you will not see the first signs.
• Tenants may not notice a slow leak in an attic, or may not mention it.
• By the time a ceiling stain shows up, there can be wet insulation and drywall behind it.
• A repair that forces a tenant out, even for a few days, costs you rent on top of the repair.

Here is what I can do for you: [YOUR OFFER, SUCH AS A ROOF INSPECTION]

You do not need to be there. With your permission, I will contact your tenant to set a time, check the roof, and email you a report with dated photos and a short video. You will see the same things I see.

Then it is up to you. If the roof is fine, keep the report for your records. If there is storm damage, the photos give you something solid to share with your insurance company. They decide what is covered. If an adjuster comes out, I can meet them at the house so you do not have to make the trip.

Many insurance policies have deadlines for reporting storm damage. I cannot tell you what yours says, so it is worth a quick call to your agent to ask.

If you would like me to take a look, reply to this email or call or text [YOUR PHONE]. All I need is your OK and the best way to reach your tenant.

Thank you,
[EMAIL SIGNATURE]

P.S. Own more than one rental in [CITY, STATE]? Send me the addresses and I will look at them on the same trip and send one combined report.

Earnings Plan

WHAT THIS IS

A one page plan that turns the income you want into doors to knock each week. The Goals tool in Archie runs the same math.

YOUR NUMBERS

• Income I want to earn this year: $__________
• My average commission on one sale: $__________
• Months I can sell this year: __________
• My close rate (sales out of every 100 appointments): __________ %

THE MATH, ONE STEP AT A TIME

1. Sales per year. Take your income goal and divide by your average commission. __________
2. Sales per month. Divide sales per year by your selling months. __________
3. Sales per week. Divide sales per month by 4. __________
4. Appointments per week. Divide sales per week by your close rate. __________
5. Doors per week. Multiply appointments per week by 10. __________

AN EXAMPLE

Goal $120,000, average commission $1,500, 8 selling months, close rate 40 percent.

• $120,000 divided by $1,500 is 80 sales a year.
• 80 divided by 8 months is 10 sales a month.
• 10 divided by 4 is 2.5 sales a week.
• 2.5 divided by 0.40 is 6.25, so plan on 7 appointments a week.
• 6.25 times 10 is about 63 doors a week.

WHERE MY APPOINTMENTS WILL COME FROM

• Doors I will knock each day: __________
• Neighbor Ring homes I will visit around each job: __________
• Referrals I will ask for each week: __________
• Calls I will make each week: __________
• Open leads I will follow up with each day: __________

Best Hours, Best Work

Not every hour is worth the same in roofing sales. This exercise puts your most valuable work into your most valuable hours.

PART ONE: FIND YOUR BEST HOURS

Write out your day from 7 am to 9 pm, one line per hour. Circle the hours when homeowners are most likely to be home and willing to talk. For most reps that is late afternoon, early evening and Saturday.

PART TWO: LIST YOUR WORK

Write down everything it takes to win and finish a job: knocking doors, setting appointments, inspecting roofs, presenting findings, paperwork, follow-up calls.

PART THREE: MARK WHAT EARNS

Put a star next to the tasks that only work when you are face to face with a homeowner. Those are the ones that create sales.

PART FOUR: MATCH THEM UP

• Starred tasks go in your circled hours. Protect that time.
• Everything else goes in the hours left over.

REMINDER: Copy the result onto your Daily Schedule Sheet each morning.
